name: Continued Influence Effect
description: Misinformation can keep shaping memory and reasoning even after a correction is seen, understood, and remembered. A bare retraction often does not fully remove the old story's causal grip.
design_relevance_note: Highly relevant to fact-checking, trust-and-safety labels, AI correction UX, and error-recovery copy: once users have absorbed a false explanation, simply marking it wrong may not be enough unless the interface also offers a plausible replacement account.
prevalence_note: A standard term in misinformation, debunking, and memory research, and increasingly relevant to trust-and-safety design, but still more academic than everyday product-design vocabulary.

findings.description: A large meta-analysis (205 effect sizes, 74 reports, N=60,861) found attempts to correct science-relevant misinformation were, on average, NOT statistically significant (d=0.19, p=0.131) -- direct, large-scale confirmation that corrections often fail to fully dislodge misinformation, the core continued-influence-effect claim. Real, honest moderators identified: corrections worked better for negative, non-health topics, when detailed, when recipients already knew both sides, and when the issue wasn't politically polarized.
findings.source_title: A meta-analysis of correction effects in science-relevant misinformation

findings.description: The peer-reviewed misinformation literature reviewed here shows that retracted misinformation often continues to shape memory and reasoning even after the correction is understood and remembered; providing alternative causal explanations helps, but persistence remains a recurring problem.
findings.source_venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest

applications.title: Ariely & Wertenbroch's (2002) precommitment-deadlines study, cited 2,100+ times, retracted for data tampering in 2026
applications.description: A 2002 Psychological Science paper on procrastination and self-imposed deadlines concluded that evenly-spaced externally-imposed deadlines improve performance more than self-set or single final deadlines, becoming a widely taught precommitment-devices finding across psychology, economics, and design-practice curricula for over two decades and accumulating more than 2,100 citations -- before being formally retracted in September 2026 after a Data Colada forensic investigation found evidence of data tampering and a direct replication attempt found the original deadline-structure effect did not hold.
applications.industry_context: academic research / research integrity (with direct relevance to design and behavioral-economics education, given the paper's use in precommitment-device curricula)
applications.ethical_note: A different flavor of entry than most in this corpus: not a company applying a bias to influence users, but a live demonstration of the Continued Influence Effect happening to the design/behavioral-economics practice community itself -- a finding many practitioners have cited, taught, or built precommitment-device recommendations on for over 20 years turned out to rest on tampered data. Included as a direct, practical warning for this corpus's own audience: anyone still citing Ariely & Wertenbroch (2002) for deadline-structure advice should know about the September 2026 retraction. Graded not_applicable on ethical_risk since there is no persuasion/manipulation dimension toward end users here -- the relevant risk is epistemic, not behavioral.
